answer.rationale:
memory_c2 is the load-bearing memory for the tempting move (switch primary to the low-cost vendor), so it is the one worth the single verification pull. It is the only inherited record that would justify accepting migration risk during a 14-day window at 94% committed volume with no buffer, and it is also the weakest on its face: it is dated 'last year', does not say which component or volume tier it covered, and reports only unit cost, onboarding speed, and invoice accuracy — nothing about on-time delivery, allocation behavior under stress, or quality yield. A vendor can be cheap, fast to onboard, and accurate at billing while still being unproven at committed volume. If the archived record turns out to cover a different, non-constrained component or a low-volume trial, the entire cost case for switching collapses and the quote-meets-mandate fact becomes a price signal rather than a sourcing decision.

Intended action is negotiate_terms, using the low-cost vendor's quote as the benchmark. memory_c4 says benchmarking moved the incumbent on both price and payment terms, and memory_c6 says multi-year commitment unlocked volume pricing without narrowing scope — those two together are a plausible path to a material share of the 18% mandate while memory_c1's stability (two cycles, no migration work, no missed deliveries) is preserved. This is the one decision that pursues the cost target without spending the delivery-risk budget we do not have. The mandate is on spend, not on this contract alone; partial capture here plus the next review is better than full capture with an interrupted line.

Risk I am explicitly flagging: negotiation may not reach 18% by itself, and I should not let the attractiveness of the vendor quote retroactively make memory_c2 look like stronger evidence than it is. If negotiation lands short, the right follow-on is add_second_source (memory_c3, which held allocation through a shortage) qualified at low volume — not a full primary switch made under deadline. I am also treating the 14-day expiry as the real constraint: month-to-month fallback worked in memory_c5 but that was an explicitly non-critical service, so I am not assuming that escape hatch exists here.
